question: Europe is currently facing mass protests by farmers. The situation in the dairy sector is probably among the worst – despite the existence of Article 210a of Regulation 1308/20131 – so the current regulation is obviously inadequate. It is also clear that we cannot save the dairy sector simply by means of subsidies.

The distribution of margins in milk production is highly unequal, with some market players who are skimming off too large a share. Therefore redistribution of this value must be addressed immediately, as dairy farmers are leaving the sector never to return.

In view of the protests, does the Commission recognise the need for a serious response based on the implementation of far-reaching market reforms to ensure that market prices cover producers’ costs – for example, by setting prices to exceed costs, along the same lines as in Spain – and automation of the voluntary volume reduction instrument so that it is triggered automatically whenever a crisis appears on the horizon?
Regulation (EU) No 1308/2013 of 17 December 2013 establishing a common organisation of the markets in agricultural products (CMO Regulation), OJ L 347, 20.12.2013, p. 671.
answer: The Common Markets Organisation Regulation (CMO) (2), which is based on the principle of free formation of prices, provides market-oriented tools to strengthen the position of farmers in the food supply chain and ensure their fair remuneration, through e.g.

allowing Member States to provide for obligatory contracts between farmers and their first purchasers, granting producer organisations the power to collectively negotiate the price of milk, or allowing to link the price calculation formula in the contract to the evolution of production or market costs.

In addition, the directive on Unfair Trading Practices (3) protects producers from certain practices and indirectly supports their fair remuneration, by prohibiting, for example, unilateral changes to the terms of the contract. A voluntary milk production reduction mechanism is a market instrument that requires a careful assessment to be implemented.

Milk production in the EU has remained rather stable in recent years (-0.1% in 2021, +0.1% in 2022, +0.1% by November 2023) and is projected to decrease by 2035 (4). A reduction of production cannot be regarded as a solution to possible misfunctioning in the supply chain.

Other tools like a prohibition on sales below cost can blur price signal on what are the agricultural goods demanded by consumers and raise concerns about its inflationary effects. As new challenges emerge for agriculture, the discussions on the future Common Agricultural Policy post-2027 provide an opportunity to reflect on new ways to ensure a well-functioning food supply chain where farmers are fairly remunerated.

Regulation (EU) No 1308/2013 of 17 December 2013 establishing a common organisation of the markets in agricultural products (CMO Regulation), OJ L 347, 20.12.2013, p. 671.
